Hi, All,

I am pretty new to Stan language although I used to have some experience in WinBUGs, but I am still learning the Stan language in R, with RStan.

Here is my detailed problem:

I am trying to examine guessing as a student characteristic in Rasch model. Rather than assuming guessing is an item parameter and is a constant across all student, I assume, more realistic, that guessing varies based on students' latent ability --- the higher the ability, the less chance for guessing. Then whether student answer one particular item correctly, is the weighted combination of guessing and their ability:

Bernoulli (gurssing_j*1/k + (1-guessing_j)*(exp(theta_j - item.diff_i)/(1+exp(theta_j - item.diff_i)))

where i is the number of items, and j is the number of students.

I generated the data in the way that I proposed [In the attached R file, line 23 - 75 is the function that I generated the data], and want to analysis the data. I think this model cannot be analyzed in traditional IRT models, because now guessing is now at the student side. Then I am trying to analysis the data with Rstan using the Bayesian approach.

So I write my model in Stan language, and try to compile it. At a start point, I started with simplest prior distribution for all parameters, and the model:

for(i in 1:n_student)
  {
    for (j in 1:n_item)
      {
        y[i,j] ~ bernoulli(guessing[i]*.2+(1-guessing[i])*inv_logit(theta[i] - item_diff[j]));
      }
  }
}

The Rstan model is actually compiled, but there is no samples when I am calling it. And I tried the same code in R on both Mac OS and Windows OS, and it turns out two different problem, but both of them has no sampling in the chain.

First, we strongly recommend taking the model code out of
the R program and making it standalone so that you can get some
use out of line numbers. I'd also strongly advise indenting
and using standard bracketing.

Also, fewer comments. I always say that comments go stale,
and here's a prime example:

item_diff ~ uniform(0 ,1); # a normal prior for the difficulty

Anyway, there are several problems with this model, the main
one of which is that you need to constrain parameters. If
you really require item_diff in (0,1) uniform, then you need
lower- and upper-bound constraints on item_diff's declaration.
Also, the "guessing" parameter is unconstrained, so you'll get
negative values unless you constrain it or put it through an
(inverse) link function yourself (inv_logit) or constrain it
to fall in (0,1).

- Bob



code_mm<-'data {
int<lower=0> n_student; # n_student: the number of students
int<lower=0> n_item; # n_item: the number of items
int<lower=0,upper=1> y[n_student, n_item]; # the matrix of responses
}

parameters {
vector[n_student] theta; // ability theta for student
vector[n_item] item_diff; // difficulty for item
vector[n_student] guessing; // guessing factor for item
}


model {
// assigning prior distribution for paramaters;
// item_diff is the item difficulty on a uniform(0,1)
item_diff ~ uniform(0 ,1); # a normal prior for the difficulty
// theta is the latent ability with mean 0 and variance 3
theta ~ normal(0,1.732); # a normal prior for the student ability
// guessing follows a prior of uniform(0,1)
// guessing ~ beta(5,23);
guessing ~ uniform(0,1);

On Friday, January 15, 2016 at 1:39:24 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:

First, we strongly recommend taking the model code out of
the R program and making it standalone so that you can get some
use out of line numbers.  I'd also strongly advise indenting
and using standard bracketing.  

Also, fewer comments.  I always say that comments go stale,
and here's a prime example:

item_diff ~ uniform(0 ,1); # a normal prior for the difficulty

Anyway, there are several problems with this model, the main
one of which is that you need to constrain parameters.  If
you really require item_diff in (0,1) uniform, then you need
lower- and upper-bound constraints on item_diff's declaration.
Also, the "guessing" parameter is unconstrained, so you'll get
negative values unless you constrain it or put it through an
(inverse) link function yourself (inv_logit) or constrain it
to fall in (0,1).

- Bob



code_mm<-'data {
int<lower=0> n_student; # n_student: the number of students
int<lower=0> n_item; # n_item: the number of items
int<lower=0,upper=1> y[n_student, n_item]; # the matrix of responses
}

parameters {
vector[n_student] theta; // ability theta for student
vector[n_item] item_diff; // difficulty for item
vector[n_student] guessing;  // guessing factor for item
}


model {
// assigning prior distribution for paramaters;
// item_diff is the item difficulty on a uniform(0,1)
item_diff ~ uniform(0 ,1); # a normal prior for the difficulty
// theta is the latent ability with mean 0 and variance 3
theta ~ normal(0,1.732); # a normal prior for the student ability
// guessing follows a prior of uniform(0,1)
// guessing ~ beta(5,23);
guessing ~ uniform(0,1);

// Likelihood:

for(i in 1:n_student)
  {
    for (j in 1:n_item)
      {
        y[i,j] ~ bernoulli(guessing[i]*.2+(1-guessing[i])*inv_logit(theta[i] - item_diff[j]));
      }
  }
}
'

> On Friday, January 15, 2016 at 1:39:24 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> First, we strongly recommend taking the model code out of
> the R program and making it standalone so that you can get some
> use out of line numbers. I'd also strongly advise indenting
> and using standard bracketing.
>
> Also, fewer comments. I always say that comments go stale,
> and here's a prime example:
>
> item_diff ~ uniform(0 ,1); # a normal prior for the difficulty
>
> Anyway, there are several problems with this model, the main
> one of which is that you need to constrain parameters. If
> you really require item_diff in (0,1) uniform, then you need
> lower- and upper-bound constraints on item_diff's declaration.
> Also, the "guessing" parameter is unconstrained, so you'll get
> negative values unless you constrain it or put it through an
> (inverse) link function yourself (inv_logit) or constrain it
> to fall in (0,1).
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
> code_mm<-'data {
> int<lower=0> n_student; # n_student: the number of students
> int<lower=0> n_item; # n_item: the number of items
> int<lower=0,upper=1> y[n_student, n_item]; # the matrix of responses
> }
>
> parameters {
> vector[n_student] theta; // ability theta for student
> vector[n_item] item_diff; // difficulty for item
> vector[n_student] guessing; // guessing factor for item
> }
>
>
> model {
> // assigning prior distribution for paramaters;
> // item_diff is the item difficulty on a uniform(0,1)
> item_diff ~ uniform(0 ,1); # a normal prior for the difficulty
> // theta is the latent ability with mean 0 and variance 3
> theta ~ normal(0,1.732); # a normal prior for the student ability
> // guessing follows a prior of uniform(0,1)
> // guessing ~ beta(5,23);
> guessing ~ uniform(0,1);
>
> // Likelihood:
>
> for(i in 1:n_student)
> {
> for (j in 1:n_item)
> {
> y[i,j] ~ bernoulli(guessing[i]*.2+(1-guessing[i])*inv_logit(theta[i] - item_diff[j]));
> }
> }
> }
